others.A: **I only.** Rejects the true III. A candidate picks this if they think the halving error compares an estimate with the true value rather than with the previous estimate. III would be false only if it said $\widehat{M}$($n$) $- M_{\text{true}}$.
others.B: **I and II only.** Accepts II, a sibling swap with LO 1.e: the halving error is a discretisation measure, not a standard error. II would be right if it read “a halving error close to zero shows that the estimate has converged in $n$”.
others.D: **I, III and IV only.** Accepts IV, a polarity flip on GARP’s comparison: the spectral measure needs a larger $n$ than ES. IV would be right if “no larger” were “a considerably larger”.

others.A: **Sibling case: size.** Rational investors bidding up a published anomaly until it vanishes is GARP’s second explanation for the disappearance of the size effect (Grossman-Stiglitz near-efficient market). It does not describe a sudden rebound triggered by bailouts, and momentum has not disappeared. A would be correct for SMB after the mid-1980s.
others.C: **Sibling case: volatility selling.** Steady premiums followed by a crash when volatility spikes is the lesson of selling volatility protection (LO 84.c: the Merrill Lynch volatility index losing nearly 70% from September to November 2008, with skewness of −8.26). GARP does not characterize momentum as a short-volatility position; it notes only that crash periods were also times of high volatility. C would be correct for a put-writing fund.
others.D: A booming economy hurting a strategy, so that the strategy needs its own definition of bad times, is the value lesson from the late-1990s Internet bull market. Early 2009 was not a boom, and the cause was explicitly a policy event. D would be correct for an HML fund in 1998 to 1999.

others.A: **Sibling swap.** “Roughly flat average returns, anomaly only in Sharpe ratios” is the pattern of the beta anomaly (returns around 15% for four beta quintiles, 12.7% for the fifth). Transplanted onto the volatility sort, it is wrong: volatility-sorted returns fall from above 10% to 0.1%. A would be correct if the stem described stocks sorted on lagged beta.
others.B: **Polarity flip.** B reverses the direction of average returns across the quintiles and invokes a “paid for risk” story. Rising returns with volatility is what clientele and noise-trader models predict for idiosyncratic volatility, but the data show “exactly the opposite.” B would describe the result only if the empirical relation had been positive, as theory in segmented markets suggests.
others.D: **Scope or condition error.** The first half is true, but D adds a condition that reverses GARP: ranking on total volatility “produces very similar results,” and Ang et al. stress the robustness of the negative relation for “both idiosyncratic and total volatility.” D would be right only if total and idiosyncratic volatility sorts gave different answers, which they do not.

others.A: A true statement (Summary and §8.7). It would be the incorrect statement if it said correlations fall in a systemic crisis.
others.B: A true statement (§8.8 conclusion; Schweser Key Concepts LO 8.g). It would be incorrect if either lever were said to raise the worst case.
others.C: A true statement (§8.8 closing paragraph). It would be incorrect if it said higher correlation lowers CVaR, or described CVaR as a market-risk measure.

MR-HQ-8g-12.why:
GARP §8.8: if the default correlation is bigger than 0 and smaller than 1, the worst case is reduced; only at a correlation of 1 is there no benefit from the lower concentration ratio.

D is the answer: error type scope or condition error, moving the boundary of the benefit from $\rho<$ 1 to $\rho$ = 0.

others.A: Consistent with GARP: a short window may not give statistically reliable estimates. It would be the answer if it said “use as few observations as possible to keep beta current”.
others.B: Consistent with GARP’s Fed example, generalized to any central bank: an earlier, similar episode can be more relevant than the recent past. It would be the answer if it said the most recent window is always the right one.
others.C: Consistent with Schweser (compare periods because $\beta$ is assumed constant) and GARP (out-of-sample checks). It would be the answer if it said beta, once estimated, never needs re-examination.

MR-HQ-11c-08.why:
D is the only recommendation that contradicts the source: GARP treats window length as a tradeoff, not a monotonic improvement.

**The answer.** Error type: absolute claim. “Always” overrides the trade-off between statistical reliability and relevance.

others.A: **Row A (sibling swap on the basis).** “Historical relationships between market variables” is the basis of the pre-GFC approach, whose failure motivated MDS. Row A would be the right description of the old regime’s basis, not of MDS.
others.C: **Row C (absolute-claim trap on subjectivity).** Statistical aggregation does not eliminate subjectivity; Schweser says it is unavoidable. Row C would be right only if the source claimed full objectivity.
others.D: **Row D (polarity flip on transparency).** The benefit of MDS is that views become transparent and open to challenge across the firm. Keeping each desk’s views confidential reverses this. Row D would be right only for a siloed process, which MDS is designed to avoid.

others.A: **Row A (sibling swap of (i) and (ii)).** Market making and liquidity security selection are exchanged. Row A would be correct if mandate (i) tilted toward illiquid small caps and mandate (ii) quoted two-way prices in corporate bonds.
others.B: **Row B (sibling swap of (ii) and (iii)).** Passive allocation and liquidity security selection are exchanged: tilting within a sleeve is selection within a class, while a strategic weight to real estate and timber is allocation to illiquid classes. Row B would be correct if the two mandates’ descriptions were exchanged.
others.C: **Row C (sibling swap of (i) and (iv)).** Market making and dynamic factor strategy are exchanged. Market making is trade by trade in individual securities; the dynamic factor strategy works at the aggregate portfolio level. Row C would be correct if (i) described aggregate long-short rebalancing and (iv) described buying from quick sellers.

CR-PY-118.concept: For $n$ positions with zero mean, equal variance and average correlation $\bar{\rho}$, the netting factor is $\frac{\sqrt{n + n(n - 1)\bar{\rho}}}{n}$: the ratio of netted to gross exposure. A lower factor means a larger netting benefit. More positions and lower (especially negative) correlation both lower it.

others.A: ABC has a higher netting factor (66.1%) than the current agreement, so the benefit gets worse.
others.B: LMN improves the factor only slightly, to 52.1%.
others.C: Correct. PQR has the lowest netting factor, 14.7%.
others.D: TUV is close at 17.1%, but its correlation is less negative, and that outweighs its two extra positions.

CR-PY-118.trap: More positions is not automatically better. The correlation term is multiplied by $n(n - 1)$, so a slightly more negative correlation can beat a larger $n$. Compute both of the negative-correlation candidates.

CR-PY-119.concept: Same netting factor, $\frac{\sqrt{n + n(n - 1)\bar{\rho}}}{n}$, with new numbers. The lowest factor gives the largest netting benefit.

others.A: L has a higher netting factor (65.7%) than the current agreement, so the benefit gets worse.
others.B: M improves the factor only slightly, to 54.8%.
others.C: P gives 19.4%, a large improvement but not the largest.
others.D: Correct. Q has the lowest netting factor, 18.5%.

CR-PY-119.trap: This is the sibling of the previous question with the outcome reversed: here the combination with more positions wins even though its correlation is less negative. The answer cannot be guessed from the pattern; both candidates must be computed.
